checks.title: Publicly accessible S3 buckets
checks.why: Anyone on the internet can read (and sometimes write) the data in these buckets.
checks.fix: Remove the public policy/ACL and turn on Block Public Access, unless the bucket intentionally hosts public files.

checks.title: Console users without MFA
checks.why: A stolen or guessed password is enough to sign in.
checks.fix: Require MFA for every IAM user with console access, or move people to IAM Identity Center.

checks.title: Security groups open admin/database ports to the internet
checks.why: SSH, RDP and database ports open to 0.0.0.0/0 are scanned and brute-forced constantly.
checks.fix: Restrict these rules to known IPs, or use Session Manager / a VPN instead.
checks.ok: No admin or database ports open to the internet

checks.title: S3 Block Public Access is off for the account
checks.why: Any bucket can be made public by a single policy or ACL mistake.
checks.fix: Turn on account-level S3 Block Public Access (SecurityStack can do this as an opt-in auto-fix).
checks.ok: S3 Block Public Access is on for the account

findings.detail: Account-level Block Public Access is not fully enabled

checks.title: Security Hub is off
checks.why: There's no continuous check of your configuration against security best practices.
checks.fix: Enable Security Hub with the AWS Foundational and CIS standards (SecurityStack does this).

checks.title: Inspector vulnerability scanning is off
checks.why: Known software vulnerabilities in EC2, container images and Lambda go unnoticed.

checks.title: IAM Access Analyzer is off
checks.why: Resources shared with outside accounts or the public aren't flagged.
checks.fix: Create an account analyzer in each region; it's free (SecurityStack does this).

checks.title: Root user has no MFA
checks.why: Anyone with the root password controls the entire account, including billing and deleting everything.
checks.fix: Sign in as root and add an MFA device (a hardware key or authenticator app).

checks.title: Root user has access keys
checks.why: Root keys cannot be limited by any policy. If leaked, an attacker has full control.
checks.fix: Delete the root access keys and use IAM roles or users with least privilege instead.
checks.ok: Root user has no access keys

checks.title: Custom policies grant full admin (*:*)
checks.why: Policies allowing every action on every resource give whoever holds them total control.
checks.fix: Replace *:* with only the actions and resources each workload needs.

checks.title: No multi-region CloudTrail trail is logging
checks.why: Without an audit trail you can't see who did what, or investigate an incident.
checks.fix: Create a multi-region trail with log file validation (SecurityStack does this).

checks.title: GuardDuty threat detection is off
checks.why: Compromised credentials, crypto-mining and data exfiltration go unnoticed.
checks.fix: Enable GuardDuty in every region you use (SecurityStack does this).

checks.title: Publicly accessible databases
checks.why: The database endpoint is reachable from the internet, protected only by its password.
checks.fix: Set PubliclyAccessible to false and reach the database through private networking.

checks.title: Weak or missing password policy
checks.why: Without a policy, IAM users can set short, easily guessed passwords.
checks.fix: Set an IAM password policy: at least 14 characters, and prevent reuse.

checks.title: AWS Config is not recording
checks.why: There's no history of how resources changed, which audits and investigations rely on.
checks.fix: Turn on the AWS Config recorder (SecurityStack does this).

checks.title: EBS encryption by default is off
checks.why: New disks and snapshots can be created unencrypted.
checks.fix: Turn on EBS encryption by default in each region (SecurityStack can do this as an opt-in auto-fix).
checks.ok: EBS encryption by default is on

checks.title: Unencrypted databases
checks.why: Data at rest and its snapshots are not encrypted.
checks.fix: Restore from an encrypted snapshot copy to encrypt an existing database.

checks.title: Unused or old access keys
checks.why: Keys unused for 90+ days are forgotten credentials that still work if leaked.
checks.fix: Deactivate and delete keys that aren't used; rotate the rest regularly.
checks.ok: No unused or old access keys
